subsystems.name: Tissue preparation
subsystems.role: preserves the brain's wiring at the moment of death or biopsy, then makes it electron-dense.

subsystems.name: Sectioning
subsystems.role: cuts or exposes the block in tens-of-nanometre steps.
parts: tape or wafer collection of thousands of serial sections

subsystems.name: Imaging
subsystems.role: scans every section into a digital image stack.

subsystems.name: Alignment and stitching
subsystems.role: registers thousands of images into one coherent volume.

subsystems.name: Segmentation
subsystems.role: traces the boundary of every neuron and process.

subsystems.name: Synapse annotation
subsystems.role: finds the actual connections and their direction.

subsystems.name: Data and compute
subsystems.role: stores and serves datasets far larger than the source tissue.

buildSteps.title: Obtain and fix tissue
buildSteps.detail: Consented surgical or post-mortem human tissue is chemically fixed within minutes so structures do not degrade; only small blocks can be handled today, typically around a cubic millimetre.

buildSteps.title: Stain and embed
buildSteps.detail: Heavy-metal stains bind to membranes and vesicles, making them scatter electrons differently; the tissue is then infiltrated with resin and hardened.

buildSteps.title: Cut into serial sections
buildSteps.detail: A diamond knife shaves sections roughly 30 nanometres thick, which are collected on tape or wafers. A block-face alternative mills away a thin layer and images the fresh surface, avoiding handling thousands of fragile sections.

buildSteps.title: Image every section
buildSteps.detail: A scanning electron microscope rasterises each section at a few nanometres per pixel. This resolves membranes and synaptic vesicles, but not molecules or atoms — 'atomic resolution' is not what this method delivers.

buildSteps.title: Align the stack
buildSteps.detail: Software registers each image to its neighbour, correcting for stretching, folding and cutting artefacts, so a single neuron can be followed from top to bottom.

buildSteps.title: Segment the cells
buildSteps.detail: Trained neural networks propose boundaries for every axon, dendrite and glial process; human proofreaders then fix the errors, which is the largest labour cost.

buildSteps.title: Identify synapses
buildSteps.detail: Regions where two processes touch and vesicles cluster are marked as connections, with direction inferred from which side holds the vesicles.

buildSteps.title: Build the graph and analyse
buildSteps.detail: The result is a directed wiring diagram that can be searched for cell types and motifs. Most projects map neurons only; glia, neuromodulators and the brain's electrical dynamics are largely absent.

buildSteps.title: Scale up
buildSteps.detail: Reaching a whole human brain would multiply the data volume by roughly a million — an order of a zettabyte of image data by simple extrapolation from published cubic-millimetre datasets — and would require imaging, storage and proofreading throughput that do not exist.

prerequisites.why: without reliable automation, millions of images per sample cannot be collected.
models are good but still need heavy human proofreading; that labour, not imaging, is the scaling wall.
a single cubic millimetre already produces petabytes, so storage and serving are proven at that size but not a million times larger.
swelling tissue inside a polymer gel lets ordinary microscopes resolve finer detail and can be combined with electron imaging, but it is not yet the backbone of large connectomes.

prerequisites.tech: Ethical access to human brain tissue
prerequisites.why: whole-brain preservation requires donation and consent pathways at a scale that does not yet exist.

pathway.milestone: complete wiring diagrams of small nervous systems and small volumes of mammalian cortex
pathway.unlocks: proof that structure can be recovered at synapse level, plus public datasets and tooling.

pathway.milestone: whole-brain connectome of a small mammal such as a mouse
pathway.unlocks: the first complete wiring diagram of a mammalian brain and much faster automated pipelines.

pathway.milestone: many human regions, and cross-referencing with non-invasive imaging and physiology
pathway.unlocks: structure–function links, and comparison of healthy and diseased tissue.

a static structural reference for the brain — a constraint on theories of how experience and cognition arise, not an explanation of consciousness, which also depends on dynamics, chemistry and glia that such a map would miss.
